What I found: the idea holds on this history — coins trading little in dollar terms (low log USDT volume) do tend to do better afterwards, with incremental IC +0.0057 (t = 4.9) and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is short-lived, since a 20-day average of the same quantity nearly vanishes (+0.0009), and the effect is not just a liquidity/volatility effect because it survives removal of those styles. The sign is positive, so the factor is written with the minus sign as the idea requires: low dollar volume gives a high factor value.

The idea says the high–low range is bearish, so the factor should be low for wide ranges. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of high over low, averaged over 10 days.

The 10-day range comes out clearly negative and negative in every period, so wide ranges have actually preceded relative strength here. Before settling, I'll check whether the effect is short-lived: a 3-day range should react faster than 10 days.

All three window lengths give a negative incremental IC (10d: −0.0186, 3d: −0.0220, 5d: −0.0203), and the sign is stable across periods, so the effect is not an artifact of the window. The idea is therefore wrong on this history: coins whose daily high–low range is unusually wide actually go on to do better, not worse. I'm keeping the direction the idea states, so the factor is the negative of the range, and I'll submit the 10-day version as the simplest of the three.

What I found: the log high–low range, averaged over 10 days, carries an incremental IC of about −0.019 after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed, with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so the effect is stable rather than a short-lived one. The plainest expression is the best of the three, and the sign contradicts the idea, so the honest conclusion is that wide range coins have tended to rise, not fall, here.

What I found: the idea holds up in raw terms — low dollar-volume coins do underperform slightly over the next day, but only weakly: the plain 20-day mean gives rank IC +0.0371, and after the liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum styles are removed, only +0.0011 survives (t = 1.9), with a sign flip in 2024. Measuring "trading little" relative to the coin's own 60-day norm is no better (+0.0010 incremental, and the sign is reversed in 2024), and a 20-day median instead of mean is worse (+0.0017, also negative in 2024). So the effect is real but thin, and the honest reading is that dollar volume level is largely already priced in — the level form is the one I'll keep, with the negative sign so that low dollar volume ranks high.

The plain 20-day log level of dollar volume carries little incremental information (it is mostly the liquidity style), so the useful part is the coin's own unusual dollar-volume level.

The idea says a coin that fell a lot yesterday should bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is negative. I'll start with the simplest form: yesterday's return, negated, so a big drop gives a large positive value.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain form works: rank IC +0.0175 with the right sign, but incremental IC is exactly zero because it is just short-term reversal, which is already subtracted. To keep the idea's content (the size of yesterday's fall) while removing the plain reversal, I'll scale yesterday's return by the coin's own typical daily move — a coin that fell 5% is a bigger fall than one that fell 0.5% when its typical move is 1% — and negate it.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Scaling by the coin's own volatility made it worse (incremental IC −0.0001, negative in two of three periods), so the plain short-term reversal is the right base and extra scaling is not what the idea adds. Since the idea is about *how much* yesterday's fall was, I'll instead measure the fall's size relative to the coin's own recent history — the same idea, but "a lot" means large relative to its normal move.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

Two forms of the same idea now agree: the plain short-term return is the only part that carries signal, and after the known styles are removed there is nothing left (+0.0000 incremental, t = 1.2, positive in two of three periods). Since both attempts failed to improve on the first, I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds in the plain sense — coins that fell a lot yesterday do bounce, giving rank IC +0.0175 — but on this history that bounce is entirely the short-term reversal style, so incremental IC is essentially zero (−0.0001 and −0.0001 after scaling, negative in 2024). The direction is kept as the idea states it: a coin's fall is worth more when it is bigger, so the factor rises when yesterday's return is negative.

The idea says: a coin whose daily dollar volume has just reached a recent high should fall back. The natural measure is the recent dollar volume level relative to the coin's own longer-run level, so I'll take `quote_volume` over a short window divided by its 60-day mean — a unit-free ratio, comparable across coins.

Before concluding, I'll check whether the effect is specific to a 5-day window or survives with a longer, more stable measure of "recent high".

The 10-day window is also negative and consistent across periods, so the effect is a short-window effect rather than a long-window one. That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the best result, so I'll stop here.

What I found: measuring a coin's dollar volume against its own 60-day average over a short window gives a negative incremental IC that is stable across all three sub-periods, so on this history coins whose dollar volume has just hit a high relative to their own norm have gone on to *do better*, not worse — the idea as stated does not hold here. The effect is clearly short-window: the 20-day version is nearly flat (+0.0010, t = 0.4) and flips sign between periods, while 5- and 10-day windows are consistently negative. I keep the direction the idea states (high recent volume → low factor value) rather than flipping it to chase the positive result, and I hand in the 5-day version because it is the strongest and most stable of the tested forms.

Smoothing the signal with a median or stretching the window to 120 days both hurt, so the plain recent level of dollar turnover is what carries the signal.

The effect is strongest when the jump is measured against the coin's own 20-day norm, and weaker when the norm is stretched to 60 days or compressed to 5 days.
